name: Vitamin D and B12 deficiency (diet follow-up)
surveyQuestion: Do you have any of these health conditions? (select all that apply) -> Vitamin D deficiency / Vitamin B12 deficiency. Check question: Has a doctor or lab report told you that your vitamin D or vitamin B12 is low? Yes, vitamin D low / Yes, B12 low / Yes, both / Yes, borderline (lifestyle-only mode) / No / Never tested (suggest asking a doctor if symptoms) / Not sure. Follow-ups: diet pattern (vegetarian, eggetarian, non-veg, Jain, vegan); latest 25(OH)D and serum B12 with units and date (enter or skip); Do you take any vitamin D or B12 tablets, sachets or injections? No / Yes (enter product, amount and unit, how often) / Not sure; Do you take metformin or acidity medicines (PPIs such as pantoprazole, omeprazole)? No / Yes / Not sure; hours outdoors in daytime and whether most skin is covered; Do you have tingling, numbness, balance problems or memory changes? No / Yes (shows doctor prompt); Are you pregnant or breastfeeding? No / Yes

bloodMarkers.target: Below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL): risk of deficiency; 30 to under 50 nmol/L (12 to under 20 ng/mL): inadequate for some people; 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) or more: adequate for most; above 125 nmol/L (50 ng/mL): possible harm. Many Indian lab reports use 30 ng/mL as sufficient; an Indian expert consensus (2025) aims for 40-60 ng/mL (100-150 nmol/L) (secondary). Doctor interprets
bloodMarkers.source: NASEM/NIH ODS; Endocrine Society 2011 cut-offs via Indian consensus (<20 deficiency, 21-29 insufficiency, 30+ sufficient; secondary); Kalra et al., Indian J Endocrinol Metab 2025 (secondary)

bloodMarkers.target: Below 200 pg/mL (about 148 pmol/L): deficiency; 200-350 pg/mL: possible deficiency, check MMA; Indian studies often use below 150 pmol/L; labs differ
bloodMarkers.source: Cochrane (Wang 2018) used below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L); NICE CKS (below 200 ng/L); thresholds via secondary summaries

bloodMarkers.target: Above about 260 nmol/L suggests B12 deficiency in one study; cut-offs vary by lab; doctor interprets
bloodMarkers.source: Published study cut-offs via secondary summary (secondary, unverified)

bloodMarkers.target: Above about 12 to 15 µmol/L raised in B12 deficiency (cut-offs vary by lab; also raised by folate or B6 shortage and kidney disease)
bloodMarkers.source: Published study cut-offs via secondary summary (secondary, unverified)

bloodMarkers.target: Low haemoglobin with large red cells (high MCV) can point to B12 or folate deficiency, but nerve damage can occur with a normal MCV (about 25% per CKS)
bloodMarkers.source: NICE CKS (via summary); see P11 for haemoglobin cut-offs

waterMl.notes: No change from FitPlate general adult water target. Drink more in heat, exercise or fever per general rules. Vitamin D excess can cause thirst and passing a lot of urine, which is a reason to stop and see a doctor, not to drink more. Pregnancy, heart, kidney or liver disease, kidney stones or water pills: general range only, never a higher target. Follow your doctor's advice.

conflictsWith.rule: Vegan: food cannot meet the B12 target; always show 'ask your doctor about a reliable B12 source such as fortified foods or a supplement'; do not suggest milk, curd, eggs or fish; vitamin D food options are limited to fortified products, so keep the doctor prompt
Jain: dairy is the only natural B12 source, so suggest 2-3 servings of milk, curd or paneer a day; no eggs, fish or meat suggestions
Pregnancy: requires doctor input; B12 2.6 µg (NASEM) and vitamin D 15 µg from food; never set supplement doses; pregnancy overrides P12
Breastfeeding: requires doctor input; B12 2.8 µg (NASEM); baby's B12 depends on the mother; doctor review
Chronic kidney disease: doctor-led vitamin D handling; avoid high-dose B-vitamin combinations unless prescribed (DIVINe trial); P13 overrides potassium, fluid and supplement messages
Kidney stones: vitamin D and calcium products need doctor advice; show the vitamin D total against the 100 µg UL; never push a higher fluid target
Type 2 diabetes on metformin: show a one-time 'ask your doctor about a B12 test' card (MHRA 2022); no change to targets
Acid reflux on long-term PPIs or H2 blockers: show the same B12 test prompt; crystalline B12 in fortified foods is less affected (NASEM)
Osteoporosis: vitamin D and calcium together; keep calcium food target 1000 mg; supplements are the doctor's decision
Iron-deficiency anaemia: compatible; B12 deficiency often co-exists; suggest asking the doctor whether B12 was checked; iron rules from P11 still apply
Celiac disease, IBS or bowel surgery: absorption of B12 and vitamin D may be reduced; doctor input needed; no dose advice

warnings: General information, not medical advice; FitPlate does not diagnose vitamin D or B12 deficiency
Treatment doses (60,000 IU sachets, B12 tablets or injections) are set by a doctor; the app logs them without judging them
Tingling, numbness, balance or walking problems, memory change or confusion: see a doctor soon; nerve damage from B12 deficiency may not fully reverse
Vitamin D UL is 100 µg (4,000 IU) a day from all sources; repeated mega-dose courses or injections can cause high blood calcium
Do not take folic acid alone if B12 deficiency is possible; it can hide it
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and teenagers, kidney disease, metformin or PPI use: doctor input needed
Food alone rarely fixes vitamin D deficiency, and vegans cannot meet B12 from unfortified food
